bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker hears the cuckoo's cry and turns to gaze toward the direction whence it came, seeking the bird itself
bipartite.shimo_theme: Instead of the bird, only the lingering dawn moon remains in the sky
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku sets up an act of looking (眺むれば) directed at the place where the cuckoo's song was heard; the shimo-no-ku reveals what that gaze actually discloses — not the bird itself but only the moon of the fading night, producing a quiet anticlimax of absence and lingering light. The whole poem hinges on the disjunction between auditory expectation (the bird's cry) and visual result (its absence, replaced by the moon).

kigo.note: The cuckoo (hototogisu) is one of the most iconic summer kigo in classical waka, prized for its brief, elusive cry that poets strain to hear at dawn or dusk; its fleeting, half-heard song conventionally symbolizes transience and longing. Although 有明の月 (the dawn moon) is also present and often associated with autumn partings, here it functions within a summer night scene as the residual image left after the cuckoo's cry, so the cuckoo remains the dominant, poem-defining seasonal marker.
